# The Strange Beauty of Noticing Things

I've been thinking lately about how much of life happens in the margins—in the moments we're not supposed to pay attention to, the details that don't make it into conversation, the small observations that seem too trivial to mention. Yet these are often the things that stick with us longest, that shape how we actually experience the world rather than how we think we're supposed to experience it.

There's this particular quality of light in late afternoon that I've noticed more as I've gotten older. It's not the golden hour that photographers chase—it's earlier than that, when the sun is still relatively high but the angle has shifted just enough that it doesn't wash everything in uniform brightness. Instead, it creates these pockets of shadow and illumination, making ordinary things look textured in ways they don't at noon or dusk. A brick wall becomes almost three-dimensional. The weave in a cotton shirt becomes visible. Trees cast shadows with actual depth. This light lasts maybe twenty or thirty minutes, and I've started to recognize it, to pause when I see it, to just stand there and look around.

I mention this because it's the kind of thing that seems embarrassingly small to talk about in conversation. If someone asks me what I did today, I don't say, "I stood outside and noticed the light." That would make me sound either pretentious or unmoored from normal concerns. But the truth is, those moments of noticing have become more valuable to me than many of the things I'm supposed to find important.

This connects to something broader I've been thinking about: the difference between experiencing life and narrating life. We're all constantly narrating our lives now, translating moments into social media posts, into stories we tell friends, into the mental narrative we maintain about who we are and what our life is like. This narration is necessary, even valuable—it's how we make meaning, how we connect, how we create continuity between past and present and future. But it also filters experience through a lens of what's shareable, what's coherent, what fits the story we're telling about ourselves.

The things that don't fit the narrative are often the most interesting.

I think about this when I'm reading older literature—not historical fiction, but actual old writing, where the conventions were different. Medieval or Renaissance writers would include seemingly random details about what someone was wearing, or how a room smelled, or what a character noticed about another character's fingernails. These details don't advance the plot. They don't establish character in the way modern writing does. They just sit there, little fragments of sensory experience that the writer thought was worth recording. And I find myself drawn to them precisely because they feel real in a way that a more polished narrative doesn't.

Maybe this is what older people mean when they talk about having a different perspective on time. It's not that time actually goes faster as you age, though it feels that way. It's that you stop living entirely for future moments—the next milestone, the next achievement, the next chapter—and start noticing that the present moment is actually where you're living. It's obvious when you say it out loud, but it's a surprisingly difficult thing to internalize. For most of my life, I was always already somewhere else mentally: already in college, already in my career, already thinking about what would come next. The present was always just the waiting room for the future.

I wonder what kind of people we'd be if we could really live in the present without that particular neurosis—if we could be fully where we are without simultaneously reaching toward where we think we should be going. Maybe we'd be more present with other people. Maybe we'd ask better questions, listen better, notice when someone's tired or worried without them having to say it. Maybe we'd notice our own fatigue and worry too, rather than pushing past them in service of the narrative of productivity and progress.

There's something I've noticed about conversations with people who seem genuinely comfortable with themselves: they ask good questions and then actually listen to the answers. They don't seem to be waiting for their turn to talk or mentally categorizing things in terms of how they relate to their own life. They're just there, receiving what the other person is saying. I've always envied this quality. I've also noticed it's rare. Most conversations, including my own, are more like two people taking turns broadcasting their internal monologues.

This might be why I find myself drawn to nature more now—not hiking or extreme experiences, just being outside, walking, noticing things. A crow doing something complicated with a piece of bread. The particular architecture of a specific tree. Lichens on a rock. Clouds that are just clouds, not metaphors or Instagram moments. The things are just themselves, not narrated, not trying to be something other than what they are.

I think this is why I'm also more skeptical now of the constant pressure to turn everything into a story, into a lesson, into something that advances the narrative. Not every moment needs to mean something. Not every experience needs to be integrated into the larger arc of "my life." Some things can just be small, singular, unrepeatable moments that happened and then passed. There's something peaceful about that. It takes pressure off.

I've also been thinking about how much of what we worry about is actually a failure of imagination—not imagining bad things, but failing to imagine that things could be otherwise, that we could have different habits and priorities and relationships to time itself. We inherit assumptions about what life should look like, how success should feel, what matters, and we defend these assumptions as if they were natural laws rather than cultural choices. But they're not. They're choices that previous generations made, and we're under no obligation to keep making those same choices.

This sounds grandiose, but I mean it very simply: you can choose to stand outside and look at light. You can choose to notice things that don't go in any story. You can choose to be uncertain and to sit with that uncertainty rather than rushing to resolve it into a narrative. You can choose to be slower, in a world that profits from your hurrying. 

None of this will change your life in the dramatic way that we think change should happen. But maybe that's fine. Maybe the good life isn't a story arc with a satisfying resolution. Maybe it's just this—the quality of attention you bring to whatever ordinary moment you're in, the permission you give yourself to notice small things, the willingness to stand in the light for no reason at all.
